reach.rationale: Every framework API in use — App Router, segment config, navigation hooks, metadata, Turbopack root config — has been stable for a year or more; nothing experimental, preview, or recently-stable (<6 months) appears.

evidence: app/next.config.mjs:7-9 — the one config option that was once experimental (turbopack.root) is isolated to a 10-line config file
app/lib/api.js:13 — plain `fetch(url, { cache: 'no-store' })` plus an in-process Map cache; no framework caching directives anywhere
containment.rationale: Nothing experimental is used, and the closest-to-new surface (the Turbopack config) sits in a single tiny config file that would be trivial to swap.

evidence: app/app/page.jsx:10 and app/app/pokemon/[name]/page.jsx:26 — force-dynamic satisfies the spec's 'fetch at request time' requirement without reaching for use cache / cacheComponents

justification.rationale: No experimental APIs are used at all; each stable API chosen is the boring, documented fit for the job, and the app even skips the newly-recommended Cache Components model in favor of the long-stable one.

findings.issue: The app uses the classic dynamic-rendering model (`force-dynamic` + fetch no-store) rather than Cache Components, which Next.js 16.4 (Oct 2026) now recommends and enables by default for new apps.
findings.suggestion: Not a defect for stability — this is the risk-free choice — but budget a future migration to Cache Components when upgrading to Next 17, where it becomes the default.

summary: The app rides exclusively on long-stable Next.js and React APIs: App Router, segment config, navigation hooks, metadata, and one stable Turbopack config option. There are no experimental, preview, RC, canary, or recently-stable APIs anywhere in app source. This is a maximally conservative, low-breaking-change posture for a codebase owned for years.
